```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))

res <- "results"
gc <- read_csv(file.path(res, "genes_by_community.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
go <- read_csv(file.path(res, "genes_by_outcome.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)
sp <- read_csv(file.path(res, "species_by_outcome.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
cs <- read_csv(file.path(res, "contrast_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
grp <- read_csv(file.path(res, "sample_groups.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
tg <- read_csv(file.path(res, "top_gene_counts.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
n_sig <- function(x) sum(x$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## This morning you built a column {.center}

```{r}
#| echo: false
grp |> filter(time_point == "week_18") |> count(community) |> kable()
```

37 anaerobe-dominant samples and 120 Lactobacillus-dominant samples, at week 18.

. . .

Built from the **species** table. We are about to test the **gene** table with it.

## The question {.center}

For each feature, is its count systematically different between two groups of
samples?

. . .

Fourteen thousand features. One question, asked fourteen thousand times.

## Why not just run a t-test {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Counts are not normally distributed. They are bounded below by zero and skewed.
- The variance depends on the mean. A gene at 10 counts and a gene at 10,000
  counts behave differently.
- Library sizes differ, so raw counts are not comparable between columns.
- With 14,000 tests, estimating each feature's variance from 157 samples
  independently is wasteful.
:::

## The variance really does track the mean

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.8
gc |>
  filter(!is.na(lfcSE), baseMean > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(baseMean, lfcSE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.8, colour = pal[["navy"]]) +
  geom_smooth(colour = pal[["orange"]], linewidth = 1.3, se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "mean count across samples (log scale)",
       y = "uncertainty in the fold change (log scale)")
```

Low-count features carry more uncertainty. A good method knows this and borrows
information across features.

## Three lines {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(DESeq2)

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = gene_counts,          # features x samples, raw counts
  colData   = sample_table,         # one row per sample, same order
  design    = ~ community
)

dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("community", "anaerobe", "lactobacillus"))
```

. . .

Raw counts go in. Never CPM, never logged. The method does its own
normalisation, and feeding it normalised data breaks it.

## What those three lines did {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
1. **Size factors.** Worked out how deeply each sample was sequenced, so columns
   become comparable.
2. **Dispersion.** Estimated each feature's variance, then pulled extreme
   estimates toward the trend you just saw.
3. **Test.** Fitted a model per feature and tested whether the group term is
   zero.
:::

## What comes back {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
gc |> filter(!is.na(padj)) |> arrange(padj) |>
  transmute(gene = symbol, baseMean = round(baseMean), log2FoldChange = round(log2FoldChange, 2),
            stat = round(stat, 1), pvalue = format(pvalue, digits = 2), padj = format(padj, digits = 2)) |>
  head(6) |> kable(align = "lrrrrr")
```

::: {.incremental}
- `log2FoldChange` of 1 means twice as much. Of -1, half as much.
- `pvalue` is per feature, before any correction.
- `padj` is what you report.
:::

## Fourteen thousand tests {.center}

If nothing at all were different, how many features would have `pvalue` below
0.05?

. . .

About **687**.

. . .

That is why `padj` exists. Benjamini-Hochberg asks for a different promise: of
the features you call significant, roughly 5% are wrong.

## The result

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 5
gc |>
  filter(!is.na(padj)) |>
  mutate(call = case_when(padj >= 0.05 ~ "not significant",
                          log2FoldChange > 0 ~ "up in anaerobe",
                          TRUE ~ "up in Lactobacillus")) |>
  ggplot(aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), colour = call)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("not significant" = pal[["grey"]],
                                 "up in anaerobe" = pal[["orange"]],
                                 "up in Lactobacillus" = pal[["teal"]])) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change", y = "-log10 adjusted p", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## `r scales::comma(n_sig(gc))` genes, and they are not random {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
gc |> filter(!is.na(padj)) |> arrange(padj) |>
  transmute(gene = symbol, name = str_trunc(gene_name, 46),
            log2FoldChange = round(log2FoldChange, 2)) |>
  head(7) |> kable(align = "llr")
```

Mucins, filaggrin, cornified envelope proteins. Epithelial barrier genes, higher
where Lactobacillus dominates.

. . .

We did not put that there. It came with the real samples.

## Always plot the top hit {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 4.8
tg |>
  mutate(lab = paste0(symbol, "  (log2FC ", round(log2FoldChange, 2), ")")) |>
  ggplot(aes(community, normalised_count, fill = community)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.75, width = 0.6) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.35, size = 1) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(anaerobe = pal[["orange"]], lactobacillus = pal[["teal"]])) +
  facet_wrap(~lab, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "normalised count (log scale)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

All three fold changes are negative, and all three boxplots are higher on the
right. The picture and the sign agree.

## Check that every time {.center}

Getting the direction of a contrast backwards is the most common error in this
analysis.

. . .

It does not produce a warning, it does not look wrong in a table, and it
survives peer review regularly.

. . .

One boxplot catches it.

## Significant is not the same as large {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
cs |>
  mutate(contrast = recode(contrast,
    genes_by_community = "genes ~ community (from the 16S table)",
    genes_by_outcome   = "genes ~ birth outcome",
    genes_by_bv        = "genes ~ Nugent-defined BV",
    species_by_outcome = "species ~ birth outcome")) |>
  transmute(contrast, `features tested` = scales::comma(features_in),
            samples, `padj < 0.05` = scales::comma(n_sig),
            `and |log2FC| > 1` = scales::comma(n_sig_lfc1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

. . .

Read the last two columns of the first two rows against each other.

## The same number of hits, a different kind of hit {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**genes ~ community**

`r scales::comma(n_sig(gc))` significant

`r scales::comma(sum(gc$padj < 0.05 & abs(gc$log2FoldChange) > 1, na.rm = TRUE))` of them more than
doubled

A strong, local contrast.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**genes ~ birth outcome**

`r scales::comma(n_sig(go))` significant

`r scales::comma(sum(go$padj < 0.05 & abs(go$log2FoldChange) > 1, na.rm = TRUE))` of them more than
doubled

A weak shift in a great many genes.
:::
:::

. . .

Friday we come back to this: thousands of significant genes, and still a poor
prediction of who delivers early.

## And a warning about proxies {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
cs |> filter(contrast %in% c("genes_by_community", "genes_by_bv")) |>
  mutate(grouping = recode(contrast,
    genes_by_community = "Lactobacillus fraction, computed from the 16S table",
    genes_by_bv = "Nugent score of 7 or more, read down a microscope")) |>
  transmute(grouping, samples, `genes at padj < 0.05` = n_sig) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")
```

. . .

Two ways of asking "is this community disturbed". One of them is built from the
data you already have, and finds two hundred times as much.

## Other people's tools {.smaller}

We used DESeq2 on both tables, because the point this week is that both tables
are count tables. That is not what everyone does.

| for gene counts | for microbial counts |
|---|---|
| DESeq2, edgeR | ALDEx2, ANCOM-BC |
| limma-voom | MaAsLin 2, corncob |
| | DESeq2, still, often |

: {tbl-colwidths="[50,50]"}

. . .

The microbiome tools exist because that table is compositional and sparse in a
way gene tables are not. The argument is real and worth reading about.

## One trap, before you start {.center}

You built `community` from the species table.

. . .

Testing the **gene** table with it is fine.

. . .

Testing the **species** table with it is not. You would be asking whether
samples with lots of Lactobacillus have lots of Lactobacillus.

## So your exercise asks a different question {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
# the grouping comes from the clinic, not from either count table
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(species_counts, sample_table, ~ outcome)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
sp |> filter(!is.na(padj), padj < 0.05) |> arrange(padj) |>
  transmute(species = str_replace_all(species, "_", " "),
            log2FoldChange = round(log2FoldChange, 2),
            padj = format(padj, digits = 2)) |>
  head(6) |> kable(align = "lrr")
```

`r n_sig(sp)` of `r cs$features_in[cs$contrast == "species_by_outcome"]` species,
and `r sum(sp$padj < 0.05 & sp$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of them are
higher in the people who delivered early.
